analysis.one_liner: Caps PAC donations, bans soft money in federal elections, and stops lobbyists from delivering campaign checks.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal campaign finance rules. It would have cut the most a political action committee could give a candidate from $5,000 to $1,000, banned 'soft money' (big checks raised outside the normal limits and disclosure rules), and barred registered lobbyists from passing contributions to candidates on behalf of others. It also would have given taxpayers a small tax credit for donating directly to congressional candidates, required candidates to pay off campaign debts within 90 days, required House members to register their mass mailings at taxpayer expense so the public could inspect them, and required half of a candidate's contributions to come from people in the district or state the candidate is running in.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, in two ways: the rules limiting big-money influence would apply to everyone, and the tax credit would make it easier for an ordinary person's $50 check to matter. Challengers and candidates without access to PAC networks would also compete on slightly fairer terms, since lobbyists could no longer bundle checks and PAC-to-PAC money laundering would stop.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum a multicandidate PAC can contribute to a candidate from $5,000 to $1,000 [S2][S3].
Bans soft money in federal elections — money raised outside contribution limits and disclosure rules [S2][S3].

Prohibits registered lobbyists from acting as intermediaries delivering contributions to federal candidates, and limits conduits to bundling for no more than two people from the same employer or organization [S2][S3].

Provides a tax credit of up to $100 per year ($200 for joint filers) for individuals who donate directly to congressional candidates, with no credit for contributions routed through intermediary groups [S2][S3].
Caps contributions to legal defense funds set up by federal officeholders at $1,000 per person and requires disclosure of them [S2][S3].

Requires candidates to pay campaign debts within 90 days after the election and distribute leftover funds, and requires House members to register franked mass mailings with the Clerk of the House for public inspection [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees (corporate, union, and trade association), lobbying firms that bundle contributions, and the national party committees that raised unlimited soft money. Campaigns built on large PAC checks would have had to find smaller donors instead. The tax credit also costs the Treasury a small amount of revenue.

drawbacks.text: The 50% constituent-contribution requirement would have forced House and Senate candidates to raise half their money from people in their own district or state — a rule that is harder to meet in large or expensive media states and could have hobbled challengers who rely on national donor networks more than incumbents do [S3].
The tax credit adds a new cost to the Treasury and, at a $100 annual maximum, would subsidize small donations without changing the overall money race much [S2][S3].
Requiring campaign debts to be paid within 90 days after the election could have been difficult for campaigns that lose close races and face contested recounts or late bills [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — smaller PAC checks, a soft money ban, and a lobbyist bundling ban — would have reduced the influence of organized money in federal elections at little cost to ordinary people, and the tax credit would have tilted campaigns slightly toward small donors. The constituent-contribution quota is the weak part: it sounds democratic but could have penalized challengers more than incumbents, and it gives the bill a performative edge it did not need. On balance a genuine, if imperfect, reform bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, one of which passed it down to its Elections subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Tauke (R-IA) introduced the bill on June 14, 1990, and it was referred the same day to the House Administration, Ways and Means, and Post Office and Civil Service committees [S1][S5].
On July 10, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Elections of House Administration; the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action afterward [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The 101st Congress ended January 3, 1991, and the bill expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing campaign finance system and those who do well under it. PACs kept their $5,000-per-candidate channel, soft money continued to flow outside the limits, and lobbyists kept bundling checks — the rules the bill would have changed all stayed in place.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure, and the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party — a lone House Republican sponsored a reform that neither his own party nor the Democratic majority moved on.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, union, and trade association PACs)
industries.note: The bill would have cut their per-candidate limit from $5,000 to $1,000 and stopped PAC-to-PAC transfers, shrinking their role as the middleman between organized interests and lawmakers. It died, so their position was unchanged.
Registered lobbyists would have been barred from bundling or delivering contributions to federal candidates. The ban never took effect.
The bill's soft money ban would have ended the parties' ability to raise unlimited, undisclosed money for federal elections. Soft money continued to grow throughout the 1990s.

The bill would have limited their legal defense funds, barred side political committees, and required them to disclose franked mass mailings. With the bill's death, incumbents' fundraising and self-promotion tools stayed intact.
